snippet.title: LearnJavaScript.online review (JavaScript learning app for web developers)
snippet.description:
Today we’re taking a peek at an interactive JavaScript platform called LearnJavaScript.online. 
Check it out here: https://learnjavascript.online/?utm_source=rtc

What I like about these smaller platforms is that they are usually built by developers rather than a team of people who may or may not know anything about the typical self-taught developer struggle. 

As the name implies, LearnJavaScript.online is an app to help you learn JavaScript. It’s geared towards code newbies. 

This platform features interactive exercises and hands-on activities rather than videos. 

Indeed, some people prefer videos, but for others this means more active, engaged learning. And while there are both major and niche platforms that feature interactive code environments, there are a few twists to LearnJavaScript that I thought are pretty cool. 

One, you can highlight text and save it to a notes page right in the browser. 

Two there are flashcards, which sound a bit dry but actually using them they were a really nice feature.

You can also get hints and with the paid version you get a solutions box for all challenges if you get stuck. 

The first 40 lessons/challenges/flashcards are free. The remaining require you to upgrade to a pro account ($55 USD). This is a one-time charge (as opposed to a monthly/annual fee). 

One thing to keep in mind is that you must complete the challenges in the order they are presented — no bouncing around and no skipping sections. This is a nice challenge for code newbies (with the interesting stuff like projects and cool concepts like Fetch API waiting for you as a reward) but if you just need guidance on one concept, be aware of this design.

snippet.title: Real-world JavaScript interview questions
snippet.description:
Are you looking for JavaScript interview questions? If so, you have LOTS of options ranging from huge GitHub repos to blog posts filled with random JS questions to stretch your brain. 

The problem is, these questions are theoretical and while they're good to know, there's no evidence they've even been asked at interviews. 

This is where Real World JavaScript Interview Questions comes in. It's a new repo I started to share questions that were *actually* asked at interviews. 

https://github.com/RealToughCandy/real-world-javascript-interview-questions

This repo is special in a few ways. 

Firstly, these are questions submitted by interviewees. In other words, JavaScript interview questions that were actually asked. 

Secondly, they are scoured from multiple sources, including: GitHub pull requests, Twitter, YouTube, the RealToughCandy Discord, email, and more. 

Thirdly, effort is made to include contextual information in the questions. For example, how much time the developer was given to solve the problem (i.e. if it's a coding challenge) and what the job title was. 

This repo is fresh out the idea oven and already has over 40+ and multiple forks. Come be a part of a HELPFUL repo that reflects the real world! 

Please consider your support through GitHub Sponsors. For my first year, GitHub is matching all funds. Currently my work as RealToughCandy is part time. Imagine the things we could do if I was able to do this full time.

snippet.title: My dude is only making $2.50 an hour after prison & child support
snippet.description:
Yesterday I ran into an acquaintance of mine I met while working a temp job. Earlier this year I had a HUGE case of "cabin fever" and just needed to get out for a few hours. **open me**

So rather than walk around in the cold and complain about the windchill, I decided to go work some manual labor temp jobs for a few hours a week. One of my tasks was making boxes. At the box station, I met another worker, Preston. 

Preston had gotten into some trouble with the law, and was part of a prison-to-work program. He LOVED to talk, so I got to hear his life story. 

We parted ways after I shook my Cabin Fever and I haven't seen him since. That is, until yesterday when I was out browsing at a thrift store. He spotted me and gave an update on his life situation: he was still on prison-to-work, and also still paying child support. 

Currently, his take home pay is hardly enough to buy basic groceries let alone other essentials. In this video I'm sharing Preston's story and how a tech career can be a solution to poverty. Now maybe it can't solve the levels of problems Preston is currently facing, but for many of us, it can be an "out" when all we see around us are dead ends. ...Dead end jobs, dead end income, dead end choices.

Don't give up your dream of being a software developer. It's closer than you think.

snippet.title: Udemy instructors have been red pilled. We are LEAVING!
snippet.description:
A few days ago, Udemy went live with their new coupon system for instructors. 

Now, you may not think Udemy coupons are that big of deal. But for thousands of instructors who have websites, YouTube channels and other social media accounts, they are the lifeblood of our work. 

The big problem is that Udemy has now set strict timeouts for their coupons. For example, the coupons I’ve been creating & using that were set to never expire, now expire in 5 days. 

There’s no way I can go to every YouTube description box every 5 days and update my link to continuously offer a $9.99 price. That’s especially true now because I can only create 3 coupons per month!

A lot of people now simply pass on buying our courses. Worse, they're going to be even more tempted to find the course on a torrent site where creators earn nothing. Zilch. Nada.

Personally, my sales have plummeted since the new coupon system’s been revealed. It’s already hard making a buck on Udemy, and for many instructors, this could be the final straw. It definitely is for me! I was set to put the finishing touches on a UX/UI course for web developers but after this announcement I am forced to shelf the project for now until I find a viable alternative. 

WTF Udemy. Give us our coupons back!

snippet.title: As a junior developer are stacks really that important?
snippet.description:
STACKS. It's what you learn in coding bootcamp. It's what we learned with Colt Steele. And honestly, it's every employer's fantasy that each job candidate has extensive experience with the JAM, ELK, MEAN, MERN and LAMP stacks. 

But as junior developers are they really that important? Are stacks the all-powerful thing in the real world of software development?

...It depends. 

~If you're billing yourself as a full-stack developer (and looking for jobs that require knowledge of a stack), they are super important. 

However, for most of us focusing on either frontend development or backend development, the stack quickly becomes a "supporting player" when we're showing off our main competency. 

For example, if you're an Angular dev, that database integration in one of your portfolio projects isn't front and center. Rather, your Angular skills are.

That said, when every employer looking for a frontend developer gives priority points to devs with SQL chops, what's the best course of action? We're talking about it today on the RealToughCandy channel.

snippet.title: Expert warns JAVASCRIPT will be DEAD in 10 years!
snippet.description:
▶ Check out my gear on Kit: https://kit.com/RealToughCandy

No, not kidding. JavaScript will be dead in 10 years. All but replaced by other languages compiling down to WASM and using that to run on browsers. This is according to a knowledgeable and experienced web dev who was the former tech lead for NPM’s CLI. She’s also been in open source software for over a decade and I got to ask her anything!

Should we panic?  Dump JavaScript before JavaScript dumps us? Drop everything and embrace WASM?

 _heart palps_

Here’s the kinda, sorta good news: This happens to every programming language. Ever programmed in Pascal or COBOL? Most of us haven’t, but there was a time when those languages were HOT. They peaked, there are legacy apps that use them, but bigger and better things came along. As programmers we adapt and overcome. Our common goal is efficiency, and nothing is going to stop that objective. 

The inevitable decline of JavaScript is, well… inevitable. 

The wild web has always been untamed. If it’s one thing all devs can agree on, things here change constantly. But JavaScript is everywhere. So how can it possibly receding into the dark corners of our binary basements? In today’s video we’re talking about it and why you shouldn’t freak out…just yet.

snippet.title: Grandma trespasses at condos to explain VPS vs shared hosting
snippet.description:
Today we’re stopping by the 55+ community condos to explain VPS vs shared hosting. 

RealToughCandy goes incognito as Mrs. Lorraine Dobber to illustrate how VPS vs. shared hosting is much like condos vs apartment living.

Condos: Shared land but more privacy, heightened security, and freedom to paint your master bedroom any neon colors of your choosing. 

Apartments: Lots of shared resources, more limits, one bad tenant can make life miserable, but boy is it cheaper than across the tracks!

It isn’t that shared hosting stinks, or that VPS is always the right choice. It all depends on what you need and expect. 

Do you have low traffic sites with not a lot of data? 
Go for shared hosting. 

Needs lots of room for growth, root access is a must, and better security & privacy would be nice? Expecting some decent traffic? 
Go VPS.

snippet.title: What is a front end developer? || Front end developer skills 2019  || Freelance Newbie Podcast
snippet.description:
Front-end web developers — we’ve heard the term, but what exactly do they do? According to Wikipedia, “Front-end web development is the practice of converting data to graphical interface for user [sic] to view and interact with data through digital interaction using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.”

That all sounds good on paper, but when you start reading the job descriptions for front-end developer positions, things start getting a little dubious. The job requirements for one front end developer position compared to another job position are often a night-and-day difference. Many other times, it seems as if they’re not even in the market for frond-end developers, but rather looking for full-stack devs. 

So what’s up with this? How can front end developers navigate the freelancing world, which is also increasingly demanding full-stack knowledge? 

Should front end developers, specifically freelance front end developers, consider ditching learning those deep concepts React Hooks, JavaScript theory and whatever else end instead and go all in with databases, PHP and Node? We’re talking about it in today’s Freelance Newbie podcast! 

Our newest supporter is Ruben! Thank you so much! Developers, please help keep the lights on — even a buck helps!https://www.patreon.com/realtoughcandy

snippet.title: Freelance Coding: How to make money WITHOUT clients || Freelance Newbie Podcast with RealToughCandy
snippet.description:
Welcome to episode 4 of the Freelance Newbie podcast. In this edition we’re talking about making money _without_ clients. 

Wait…Huh? 

That’s right, we’re pushing the boundaries of what it means to be a freelancer, and to steal some database lingo, we’re taking traditional one-to-one relationships (where we work one-on-one with clients) and transforming it into a one-to-many relationship (where we sell the same code to multiple people). 

Taking the non-client freelance approach can be appealing for many reasons. If you aren’t a people person, have social anxiety or live in a small town where in-person freelancing isn’t doable, a one-to-many freelancing gig may be just the ticket. 

Aside from selling your code, themes, backend tech and so on at popular sites like Theme Forest, you can also take a page from popular open source developers who receive donations for their contributions. 

In this episode, we’re talking about the main challenges of getting started with selling your code on a 3rd party site, while touching upon what you can do to make your experience a profitable one. From social proof to guerrilla marketing, there are many things you can do to start getting noticed. 

In addition, we also talk about the donation route, where people pledge to support you for your efforts. While we discuss a high-profile account that earns over $16,000 a month, we also talk about the hundreds of other developers who are also getting paid for sharing their tools and techniques with the rest of the world.

It may seem odd that people get paid for their code that they published *for free*, but there are thousands of people out there who want to show their financial support as a token of appreciation. 

As always, Celina the cat is excited to add her thoughts in this episode. 

We’re stuck with each other for an hour! So come on in and get settled as we talk about this lucrative alternative way to earn income as a freelancer.

snippet.title: Guess how much Vue’s developer makes every month? || Open Source Web Developer Earnings
snippet.description:
It’s no secret that software developers can make beaucoup bucks. But just how big are we talking? 

Well, the developer of Vue has an ongoing Patreon campaign, and the numbers are looking pretty legit. We’re going to do the big reveal today, the video starts right now. 

What are some real-world open-source web developer earnings? Look no further than Even You’s Patreon page. Evan You is  the developer responsible for Vue, a frontend JavaScript framework. 

In many ways easier to learn than React, Angular, and other popular frameworks, in addition to having some impressive performance metrics, Vue took GitHub by storm and has been one of the hottest JavaScript developments in recent memory. 

But Vue is open source, which means that it’s free for anybody to use. So how in the heck does its developer make money from it? Well, with a simple Patreon page Evan was able to secure over $17,000 per month in funding. 

From developers chipping in $10 per month to larger organizations pledging hundreds, Evan was able to raise enough money solely on Patreon so that he can work comfortably on the project full time. 
But that’s not all.

In addition to his Patreon funding, Evan’s Vue project is getting financial support through Paypal and Bitcoin. 

There are probably other revenue streams coming in as well! It goes to show how profitable a project can be, even if it’s open source and free to the public. Provide value, provide a solution to a problem and the money will follow, even if there’s no price tag on it.

snippet.title: JavaScript questions & explanations || Best of GitHub || javascript-questions repo
snippet.description:
Welcome back to another episode of Best of GitHub where we explore the best repos on GitHub.  👉👉👉

There are literally millions upon millions of public repos on GitHub, and most of the time we find ourselves not needing most of them…Yet we know there must be some good stuff floating around GitHub land. This series showcases a few of those  excellent repos that can  really help developers do their jobs! 

In today's episode we're exploring a repo simply called javascript-questions. As you may have guessed, this repo consists of...dun dun dun...JavaScript questions! But not just that, these questions have thorough explanations in the answer section. 

All multiple choice, these JavaScript questions focus largely on the theory behind the language. This is a welcome relief from many other questions out there, which tend to be more trivia-based. 

For example, one question I see often is the palindrome challenge where you're asked to write a program that can identify a palindrome (a word that is spelled the same both forwards and backwards, for example "radar.") While interesting, these types of questions are not much more than trivia -- who are they really helping, what skills are they actually showing? With this javascript-questions repo, it goes deeper into the theory and you have the chance to eliminate answers via multiple choice, giving your brain a chance to flex its JavaScript skills. 

Check out the javascript-questions repo here: https://github.com/lydiahallie/javascript-questions

snippet.title: What makes developers want to QUIT? || 385 devs respond! || Self-taught web developer stories
snippet.description:
What makes you want to walk away from coding? Well, nearly 400 code newbies recently answered that question, and dozens of people sounded off. 👉

From family obligations to imposter syndrome to just too much stuff to learn, in this video these developers are sharing exactly what’s getting under their skin.

Stack Overflow's yearly survey consistently reports that the overwhelming majority of developers consider themselves at least partially self-taught. In other words, most developers who considered themselves self-taught eventually got tech jobs (this is great news). 

So what exactly is a self-taught developer and why do we have struggles? 

A self-taught developer usually doesn’t have a college degree in computer science or other tech-related subjects or they don't have a degree at all. These devs have learned to code while working, taking care of their family, along with other life obligations. 

The amount of self-determination and focus is massive for self-taught developers, plus time management is another critical factor. As we discuss in this video, it's way too easy to get lost in the rabbit hole of computer science and web development technologies and concepts. There is just so much to learn! 

Check out today's video and you'll hear dozens of self-taught developer stories where they share their challenges with honesty and insight.

snippet.title: Oh crap, here comes *another* JavaScript framework || SVELTE || Sveltejs
snippet.description:
Developers, we all knew this day was coming in the frontend framework wars. There’s a new frontend framework soaking up the spotlight -- it’s called Svelte. Is it a fad, or is it the future of web development?

Check out the talk by Rich Harris, Svelte's developer: https://youtu.be/AdNJ3fydeao

Svelte is a radical new approach to building user interfaces. Whereas frameworks like React & Vue do the bulk of their work in the browser, Svelte shifts that work into a compile step that happens when you build your app.

Rather than applying techniques like virtual DOM diffing, Svelte writes code that surgically updates the DOM when the state of your app changes.

#sveltejs #svelte #webdevelopment

Unlike online video courses and other online materials, you can't just add a section to a physical book when the tech changes and not charge for it. . .You have to release (and sell) another book. snippet.title: The sad reality of ANY tech business || Google Graveyard
snippet.description:
KilledByGoogle.com is a graveyard and cemetery for "dead" Google projects. With over 140 projects and counting, this site is interesting from a consumer-level perspective, but also from the perspective of software developers and business owners. 

The fact is, most businesses fail within five years of opening. Within ten years, the odds are even worse. Google obviously survived to become the biggest tech company in the world, but that doesn't mean it has a 100% success rate. 

KilledByGoogle.com's Google Graveyard highlights the underbelly of tech's iceberg, illustrating how many projects are "killed" in favor of greener tech pastures -- whether it's due to lack of public interest from the get-go; a fickle tech audience always looking for the new best thing; or internal strategic objectives that place these projects on the chopping block.

snippet.title: The web just turned 30 || can we code past its problems?
snippet.description:
The world wide web just turned 30! Happy birthday, www. 

Sir Tim Berners-Lee invented the world wide web. In March of 1989, Berners-Lee submitted a proposal for the web to his boss, who called it ‘Vague, but exciting’.

By late 1990, an application called WorldWideWeb was deployed at The European Organization for Nuclear Research (known as CERN) in Switzerland. Thus, the web was born.

Berners-Lee is very transparent about what he enjoys about the web, but he’s also been around long enough to see the failings and perversities of what the web has become in a relatively short time span. He explicitly details the three major problems we’re faced with in this new era: 

"1. Deliberate, malicious intent, such as state-sponsored hacking and attacks, criminal behaviour, and online harassment.

2. System design that creates perverse incentives where user value is sacrificed, such as ad-based revenue models that commercially reward clickbait and the viral spread of misinformation.

3. Unintended negative consequences of benevolent design, such as the outraged and polarised tone and quality of online discourse.What’s sadly ironic is that if these three seemingly simple, humane bullet-points were followed, we would be without the web almost overnight."

Can the web be saved from its seemingly downward trajectory, with users' safety, security, sanity, and privacy in peril? Let's talk about it in today's video where we celebrate 30 years of the web. _Disclosure: I am an affiliate for Amazon, Udemy, Hostinger, Namecheap, Digital Ocean, Cloudways, and Educative.io. snippet.title: Goodbye, JavaScript — introducing the world’s new top language?
snippet.description:
Recently, I received an infographic from an online code school, in an attempt to get me to fork over some money to learn Python. 

According to the email, JavaScript has been dethroned — Python has taken the bejeweled crown to become the world’s new top language. Is there truth to this somewhat-outlandish claim?

The chart suggests that Python has eclipsed both JavaScript and Java,  to become the top programming language. The chart also indicates the percentage of overall question views each month on Stack Overflow, limited to high-income countries as determined by the World Bank. 

There is no doubt that Python rules the fields of data science and machine learning (ML) , but if you want to the know the most popular programming languages with a much more robust metric set, check out the chart by TIOBE. This chart ranks programming languages based on three metrics: the number of skilled engineers worldwide, courses, and third-party vendors.  

This chart is significantly different than Stack Overflow’s.

So what exactly can we conclude about these two dramatically different charts? Number one, people in rich countries asked a lot of questions about Python in 2017. Number two, despite the explosion of web infrastructure, technologies, and job openings, two non-web languages (well, at least in the traditional sense) are by far the most popular among professional developers, course offerings, and third-party vendors.

snippet.title: How to use Google Takeout  || Download your Google history
snippet.description:
Google Takeout: https://takeout.google.com

Google knows a lot about you. Like, a lot a lot. 

But did you know there’s a way to find out almost everything you’ve shared with them over the years? Whether you’re driven by curiosity, you want to use this information to help guide your online privacy efforts, or maybe you just want to download your past YouTube comments for kicks and giggles, I’m going to show you the tool to do all that and more.  

I’ve got to hand it to Google. Despite their greedy little tentacles data mining our entire lives, they’ve really got things organized. Their products are on point. They even have a service that lets you download every bit of information you’ve ever provided while using your Google account. Well, almost every bit. 

This is an app called Google Takeout. It’s totally free and its a centralized site where you can pick and choose what types of information you want to download. 

As I suggested above, there are some exceptions to the data they offer, such as the video and voice portions of a Google Hangout session. Also, if you’ve used Google services without an account or you weren’t signed in - let’s say you were on a YouTube binge and weren’t signed in - that history is indeed with Google _somewhere_, but because it’s not attached to your username, you’re not going to be able to access that. 

For account users, Google Takeout is absolutely fantastic. I know other companies also offer something similar to this, for example Facebook lets you download your account activity, but I must be on some “naughty list” or something because I keep requesting my files but I never get the email telling me they’re ready. 

Anyway, this service is so useful and if you’re a software developer it also opens up a whole new world of project ideas. There is a lot of data that you can use without asking anybody’s permission or pecking around for open source data sets, because this information is all yours. 

I hope this video was helpful. Please leave a like, comment, and be sure to subscribe to the RealToughCandy YouTube channel!

snippet.title: Coding Bootcamp 2019: Is it worth it?
snippet.description:
2017 marked the year that numerous coding bootcamps closed their doors. Since then, the number of bootcamps continues to dwindle. But, there are quite a few survivors, many that appear to be doing quite well. Is a coding bootcamp worth your money and time in 2019? If you’re an aspiring developer or code newbie, you don’t want to miss this one — the video starts right now.

 RealToughCandy from the all-new RealToughCandy.com here:

Coding bootcamps were the obsession of so many media outlets four and five years ago. One of my first big motivations to learn how to code was actually from an article I read in the New York Times. Just randomly read this article about bootcamps and was like, “I need to check this out.” While I shied away from actually enrolling in a bootcamp, I did end up applying to a few and at the very minimum it really was an influential article that exposed me to the world of software development and coding education. 

But I wasn’t the only one who got swept up in this coding fury. Coding bootcamps from NYC to LA and everywhere in between were ushering in thousands of eager aspiring developers ready to make the transition to a high-tech life with the promise of lots of jobs and high wages. But then it seemed like out of the blue almost, in 2017 there was a total shift, a Coding Bootcampocaplyse. Camps like The Iron Yard, which had multiple campuses across the United States.Camps like Dev Bootcamp, which was owned by one of the biggest and most successful test preparation and certification exam providers in America — closed. 

The list goes on. And now it’s 2019. Do people still go to these things? Are they still teaching real-world skills that can actually get you a job? Should you go to one of these coding bootcamps so that you can learn real-world skills that can get you a job?The answer to the first question is yes. The answer to the second question is yes. The answer to the third question is…a hard mayyyybeee. The good news is, many survivors of the Coding Bootcampocaplyse are not only surviving, but thriving. 

They’re teaching the hot web developer stacks, often it’s something like MEAN (Mongo, Express, Angular, and Node) or MERN (Mongo, Express, React, and Node). Many camps have also expanded to offer training for auxilary careers like UX/UI and Quality Assurance.There’s also been some promising compromises developed by some of these bootcamps. 

Bootcamps provide condensed coding education for a cost. 

Sometimes it’s worth it. 

Sometimes, not so much. 

As always, I thank you for watching, I want to hear your thoughts on this, especially code bootcamp graduates. There is a lot of talk about the camps, but let’s hear from some people who were actually there. What were your experiences? How was it better than learning on your own? Are you currently employed?

snippet.title: 4-step guide to solving coding problems (with JavaScript code examples)
snippet.description:
My early career as a self-taught software developer can be defined by three distinct traits: 

1. Absorbing and practicing everything I could, wherever I could, whenever I could, in order to understand my craft;

2. Feeling consistent urges to gouge my eyes out and go back to working at the United States Postal Service whenever a missing semicolon would break my program for six hours or more;

3. Suddenly receiving 6-10 daily coupon deals from local chain pizzerias once I started learning PHP and didn’t have the physical or mental fortitude to make dinner myself.

The first six to twelve months of learning software development on your own are brutal. Not only are you stuffing your brain to the point where it feels like it’s about to literally explode, you’re also perhaps competing with naggingly negative thoughts about your competency. 

Nothing quite destroys confidence quicker than failing a so-called simple coding challenge, or having a hard time reading JavaScript examples from the Mozilla docs.  

Going from Level 0 to Level 1 in this industry takes time, patience, and failing. Lots of failing. Leveling up here is more difficult than any other level. It’s also where most people who are trying to become developers not only quit — but stay quit. 

If you feel like you’re at that level 0 and are ready to take a step forward, today I’m going to help you by showing a four-step process to assist you in solving any single coding problem.

snippet.title: How to track your competitors with price monitoring (data scraping)
snippet.description:
In this video we are looking at how to track your competitors online pricing using a web scraper. We will set up the scrape, deploy, and finally set up a time interval so the scraper can keep us updated with any price changes. I am using a web scraper developed by Mozenda. 

Let’s say you have a business: tracking your competitor’s online activities has numerous advantages. Mainly, it gives you a way to compare your own pricing to the marketplace. 

And by tracking this information, it gives you a chance to respond to your competitor’s fluctuating prices so you can come out ahead. Let me give you an example. Let’s say you sell Beats by Dre headphones. If you data scrape your competitors, it allows you to monitor the price fluctuations. 

Maybe one day they’re charging $119.99 for a set, and the next week they’re charging $109.99 for the set. If you want to keep selling headphones, you’ll need to re-price your own supply of these. With a data scraping tool we no longer have to log on every day to all these various competitor websites and see what they’re charging, write that down, and so on.  

With data scraping we can fire up an instance of the scraper and start creating our own price database without the inconvenience of manually writing everything down. While there are numerous scrapers out there — and you can even create your own if you’re a developer, but it’ll take a while  — today I’m using Mozenda. 

This option makes things go a lot quicker. We’re going to use this scraper to gather price info and we’ll be able to monitor any changes it. The first thing we’ll do is create an Agent, which is essentially an instance of the Mozenda scraper. Then, we’ll navigate to our competitor’s website — I’m just using one today for the sake of this demo, but you can use as many competitor sites as you want. 

Now I’m going to type in the product I want to monitor — in this case it’s Beats Studio 3 Wireless. Next, I click the name of the product along with the price of the product. This is a nice feature of the Mozenda scraper — you just click, do a quick select here and there, and it’s gathering your info. 

I’m all done, so I’ll just save the Agent so it can run on Mozenda’s web interface and create a little database for me. But here’s the thing — this agent isn’t going to continuously monitor prices for me; that’s going to eat up a lot of my credits, burn up a lot of energy and other resources. So what I’m going to do is set up this agent to run every day at a certain time — we’ll say noon. 

And then I’m going to tell the program that I want any changes to my data to be tracked. So, if the price of these headphones change, I get to see it.

I’ll click the gear icon, select Schedule Agent, select my how often I want the scrape to fire, then hit save. Now I’m all set up to track important pricing information on my competitor’s website!.

So again, whether you’re a business owner needing to do research, or you’re in the research department of a larger company and your boss told you to start monitoring competitors, this style of data scraping can really help.

snippet.title: 4 hosting options for web developer projects || Shared vs VPS vs Cloud vs Managed Cloud
snippet.description:
Today I'm showing you four main hosting options for web developer projects. Whether you're needing to deploy your own freelance site for your business or get a client set up with an application ASAP, the world of hosting can be overwhelming...There are just so many options -- which one is the optimal solution? 

The options I discuss are: 

1. Shared
2. VPS 
3. Dedicated Server
4. Cloud 

There are two "flavors" we also discuss in with option #4 (cloud hosting). You can go direct to the source, such as AWS (Amazon's cloud) OR you can opt for a managed hosting solution. 

While you are given utmost control when you opt to deal with the cloud directly, there are hundreds of options and to do something as simple as downloading your source code can end up being a huge event.

Also, the more moving parts there are, the bigger possibility that something will break and the YOU are left with that liability. That can take hours and even days to fix, costing you valuable dev time. That's where managed hosting comes in.

snippet.title: Freelance web developer pricing (+ bonus mansion sighting)
snippet.description:
I used to do contract work for a gas station. But not just any gas station—this place was the highest-grossing C-store in the Midwest. ***open me***

The main reason for that was because the owner priced his gas at a penny below his competition. Thus, he was the cheapest gas station in the city. The station was featured a few times on nightly newscasts, ramping up business even more. 

I probably was there a dozen times, and without fail, there would be some sort of ridiculous mini-road-rage incident.

I’ve never seen anything like it, and honestly it was pretty depressing to see. These hordes of people were disrupting so many things, all to save literally a few cents on gasoline. 

Even though I lived nearby and had provided them services with my contract work, I made a point not to gas up there. I wouldn’t even stop to go check out their interesting inventory anymore...They had lost a loyal customer due to the change. 

Now imagine that gas station is a freelance web developer – your competition. This person has what clients need, and offers the same things you do, all at the same general quality and in the same geographical area. The only thing notably different from the average customer’s standpoint is that she’s the lowest-priced option in town. As a result, swarms of clients are headed her way.

Given this information, how do you adjust your pricing? 

Think about this one for a minute. There isn’t a right or wrong answer…

- But - 

Price-matching (or going even lower) to the lowest possible price to engage your competition is a death trap. You’re going to get calls and emails, and that’s validating! It feels like you’re getting somewhere when strangers call you asking about your web work. 

What’s not validating is that people who seek out the lowest possible price in any industry are often “tire kickers” – people who aren’t really interested in closing a deal and tend to waste a lot of time. 

You never want to “turn off” reliable clients with bottom-of-the-barrel prices inspired by your competition. Let them scape the barrel; it’s a totally different business model than what will sustain you as a capable, high-quality web developer. 

I talk about this in my upcoming guide, "9 Reasons Your Freelance Web Developer Pricing Isn’t Working (and What to Do About It)," as part of my Survival Series. These are supplemental materias to my #1 book, Freelance Newbie. Think of them as expansion packs. : )

This first release in the series will be available soon on realtoughcandy.com.

snippet.title: How do you relax as a self-taught web developer? Meet Stef
snippet.description:
This is Stef Fromme DoBid. She's my #betta fish. ***open me***

I've never had an aquarium before, not even as a kid. I never asked my mom for a goldfish or was that un/lucky kid to play a game at the traveling summer carnival and have the whiffle ball land in the betta fish cup. Nope. Fish seemed SUPER boring and I wanted little to do with them. 

Fast forward to November 2018. I found Stef at the pet store one night, but she wasn't an impulse buy. I went hope to research more about betta fish and their environment because honestly, I was _totally_ ignorant on their personality (fishality?), diet, living environment, etc. I studied up for multiple hours, watched numerous videos, and the next day went to go stock up on all the aquarium supplies I needed along with fetching Stef.

It's an unfortunate myth that betta fish enjoy small spaces and dirty water. So I started off with a 3.1 gallon tank, some live plants for shade, lots of testing equipment, a heater, two thermometers, and many other accessories to ensure Stef has a great life. 

Because the females are much less flashier than males with their coloring and body type, they are often the last ones to sell. It was pretty pathetic: her regular price was $3.99 but the pet store reduced her to $2.99 just to get her off the shelf. 

Poor thing. 

I brought her home and we've been getting to know each other. I do web development and my other tech-related stuff right next to her tank, and whenever I'm feeling stressed or just sick of staring at the computer screen, I'm hanging out with Stef. She's up at all hours of the night just chillin' and the presence of the aquarium is very relaxing.

It's _so_ important to take breaks from learning and doing web development. As an entrepreneur I'm behind the computer screen from 10 to 16 hours a day and it can get very old, very quickly. Stef Fromme DoBid is a great addition. 

P.S. Celina gets SUPER annoyed when I say, "Let's go see what your sister is up to." Heh

snippet.title: Military to software dev, my experience with “The System”
snippet.description:
Responding to a subscriber question about military bureaucracy when I served and a defining moment. How did it shape me to get me where I am today as an indie software developer & freelancer? 

Militaries can seem like faceless machines with endless resources, snaking throughout the world and into our lives in a multitude of ways. It’s easy to feel cynical.  **open me**

My first year of service, I made a terrible mistake. Fortunately, nobody was hurt but it was something I’ve regretted since it happened. I was embarrassed and disgusted knowing I had made such a stupid decision that could have ended my life or the lives of others. 

While there was no way I could “take back” that incident, I worked hard to rebuild myself. I volunteered on and off base, I focused on doing my job the best I could, and kept in regular communication with higher-ups. I wanted to get right. 

When it was time to meet with my group commander, I was terrified. Not only had I dishonored those in uniform and put peoples’ lives in jeopardy, but it was also possible I would get kicked out of the military with a dishonorable discharge. Many people before me had made the same mistake and got kicked out, no second chances. It was totally understandable, but I was hoping and praying that somehow I could redeem myself from such a fate. 

After reviewing my case, the commander showed mercy on me. I did receive a punishment (rightly) but I did not get kicked out. I went on to win multiple awards in my career field and by the time I reached my second duty station, was considered one of the best in my field by my peers and supervisors. 

Because that commander showed mercy on me, I was able to use the G.I. Bill to earn my Master of Public Policy (MPP) among other degrees, and led me to where I am today as a successful software developer and freelancer. 

THAT is the experience that put a face of humanity on the military bureaucracy. Thank you Lt. Col B. for giving me a second chance in a place that, all too often, can be cold, merciless, and faceless.

snippet.title: ⭕ Steve Jobs was a monster, but
snippet.description:
***OPEN ME*** A few months ago, I got a call from a Netflix engineering manager. It was a great chat - we talked for over an hour about tech, life, and Silicon Valley culture. 

Going into the phone call, I knew I wouldn’t work for the company out of principle — but, my mind is always open to new possibilities once new information is presented to me. 

There was a chance I could be convinced, a possibility that my opinion could sway. After the phone call though, my initial thoughts and feelings were confirmed: there was no way I would ever work for a Netflix, or Twitter, or Facebook, or whatever else big tech company. I worked too hard to dedicate 40 to 80 hours a week on somebody else’s lukewarm dream. Did I really come all this way to build algorithms that would encourage people to sit on their butts and binge watch or create social bubbles? Or work on any other person or group’s directive, for that matter? Heck no. 

Steve Jobs' outlook on life confirms my ideal. Is this a good or a bad thing? I don't know, but it's too early in the game to ask the real hard philosophical questions.

In this video, we’re taking a look at a few motivational quotes from Jobs, along with a few mean and heartless quotes from him. Yeah, Jobs comes across as a monster, but despite (or because of) this, his nuggets of wisdom really stand out. 

I love his quote on poking life and see what pops out. The malleable nature of our existence means that we all have a chance to shape our reality as individuals and as a society at large. What are you going to do with that power?

snippet.title: ⭕ Web Developer goes RAGE MODE, bans Tesla from using his code
snippet.description:
***OPEN ME***
A few days ago, I was doing my little thing-thing online and stumbled upon a very active web developer. 

If you haven’t heard of Jamie K, you’ve probably used (or at least heard of) some of the projects he’s contributed to: Babel. Yarn. Marionette. Some pretty big stuff! 

He’s also spearheaded some popular personal projects that have been getting some action. Deciding to investigate the person who was partially responsible for some of my workflow, I saw his Twitter feed. 

He was going rage mode! Something had triggered this person and Jamie was no longer licensing his code to companies ranging from UPS, to Microsoft and the Vermont state college system, to Tesla.

But can he do that? In this video, we’re exploring the meaning of the MIT license and what it means to publish your code open source using a software license agreement. 

Moral of the story? Don’t open source your code if you can’t stomach the thought of somebody you don’t agree with using it. Once the code’s out of the bottle, you can’t put it back in!

snippet.title: Software development section at Barnes & Noble || Best Web Development Books
snippet.description:
***OPEN ME*** 

For a modest section tucked away in a corner, the tech books weren't looking too shabby at my recent trip to a Barnes and Noble bookstore. I mean, I've seen worse. . .I've seen LOTS worse.

Upon further investigation, they carried your standard PHP,  your C++, your Python, and even a special appearance by YouTube's very own Stef Mischook! Indeed, there were some fun surprises along with some modern dev classics like Jon Duckett's two web development tomes. 

However, there was one *very* glaring omission from the entire section: books on actual, real-life programming. 

I'm talking CS 101 stuff.

I'm talking practical work stuff.

 I'm talking the classics. 

Where is The Mythical Man-Month or The Pragmatic Programmer? The works of Uncle Bob, Martin Fowler, et al? Or even the more challenging yet staple books, such as Donald Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming (currently 4 volumes)? 

There are sooo many books here that focus on a language's syntax rather than the principles behind the language. This isn't good for aspiring developers looking for a solid foundation to build their skills. 

What do you think? Am I being too traditionalist or does Barnes and Noble need to up their tech game? Are the best books for coders here? Let me know in the comments section!

snippet.description:

If you’ve been hanging around the channel for a bit, you know how much I _love_ Mark Myers’ noob-friendly books. 

It was actually his books that helped me learn not only HTML and CSS, but also JavaScript. Mark has a special way with new learners, and he explains things elegantly without getting lost in the fog. Indeed, you can use Python for web development — and that’s exciting! 

But for now, I bought Mark’s “A Smarter Way to Learn Python” book to quickly get a grasp of the syntax rather than programming principles. What the elders say is true — learning your second (or third, fourth, or fifth) programming language is MUCH easier than learning your first. 

If you are having problems learning JavaScript (or Python), I *highly* recommend Mark Myers’ “A Smarter Way to Learn” books. 

It’s not only a book, but also a set of online exercises that test your knowledge of what you just read. 

Thus, you’re much more likely to learn rather than convince yourself that “Yeah yeah yeah, I know what a dictionary in Python is.” 
Ten minutes later:  “Erm, diction-what?”

snippet.title: ⭕How much would you charge for this website? || Fullstack freelance web development RealToughCandy
snippet.description:
“Upwork has developers that charge $5 an hour…I guess I should just give up!” Or “I can never charge $15,000 for a website, that’s so bougie that only those fancy digital agencies can get away with that.” ***OPEN ME*** 

Not so fast. 

The amount you charge for a website isn’t based on the code you hammer out, the number of headaches you get from browser testing, or the number of times you have to override CSS rules. It's not based on what Bangladeshis or Romanians or Americans are charging. It’s based on the value you add. In other words, each feature you add is worth a dollar amount. 

But how do you estimate that? Great question! It comes down to business skills, specifically research and communication. 

In this video, we go over what it means to add value to a client’s site and why any big-dreaming freelancer shouldn’t be charging bottom-dollar for their quality work. 

I started off charging a few hundred bucks per site and it was the biggest mistake I’ve made as a freelancer. People don’t respect low-wage workers and people who are always searching for the best and cheapest deal will invariably make your life miserable by demanding more of your time and other resources. Just ask any other freelancer who deals with cheapskates! And charging rock-bottom prices is just not a sustainable career move. 

The moral of the story is, start charging what your worth and work on those business skills! YOUR skills are worth money, whether that’s your own coding skills or your business and networking skills that have helped you find a team of coders to help you with your projects.

snippet.title: ⭕I quit drinking for web development || Full stack web development 2018
snippet.description:
YESTERDAY WAS MY LAST DAY OF DRINKING FOR ONE WHOLE YEAR. Full disclosure: I love IPAs (India Pale Ales). That’s right, the dank hop infusion of a 7.1% ABV beer gives me the absolute tingles!
***OPEN ME***

But guess what? These beers are taking away from my abilities as a web developer. Drinking can quickly turn into a hobby itself, and booze in no way can make me a better web developer. So tonight is my last night of drinking for one whole year. This isn’t a new thing for me.

Early last year, in January 2017, I issued a challenge to myself: no drinking for a year. I called it the Blotto Challenge. This wasn’t a coincidence: I was just starting to get heavily involved with the meat of web development, studying and practicing various web technologies varying from plain JavaScript to the MERN stack. Even though I loved my beer, I knew it wouldn’t help me complete these projects. AT ALL. 

That challenge expired in January 2018. So, for a few months I have been imbibing. Now that I have a job, though, I’m realizing that this lifestyle choice is no longer beneficial to me. I want to be at my best for my job and that means no more indulging in one of my favorite beverages. 

I’m sharing this video to keep myself accountable. I also want people to know that it’s OK to give up hobbies or habits that are not beneficial to them, without feeling less of a person by cutting back or quitting. That is a real fear; I’ve had this fear with other not-beneficial pastimes and know how stigmatized quitting can be if you’re interested in pursuing that path.

That said, for those who do choose to imbibe, imbibe on! Maybe we can share a couple next mid-May. :) Cheers to you in May 2019!

snippet.title: ⭕My web development tech stack at work  || Vue Angular Knockout PHP Apigility DB2 AS/400 full stack
snippet.description:
As a self-taught web developer, I spent a long time focusing on the MERN stack. Guess what? My new dev job uses none of those! It’s fascinating (WOOP! New tech to learn and use!), frustrating (sigh, another large chunk of tech I’m ignorant about), and a real thrill to be able to use this new stack within an enterprise setting. 

Our tech stack consists of the following (from front to back): Vue/Angular/Knockout, PHP, Apigility, DB2, AS/400. The AS/400 is a beast of a server, but it’s from the days of proprietary tech. Thus, it uses a proprietary DBMS called DB2 (I know, right?). 

Thankfully, you CAN use SQL statements with the DB2, but it’s implementation is a real challenge. All of our front-end tech is thus restrained by the limitations the AS/400 offers. “But RealToughCandy, can’t the owner just upgrade to the cloud or something?” Not so easy when you have thirty years of data on that server. And we deal with a LOT of data. 

Despite its inherent setbacks with web work, the AS/400 is still used by a lot major corporations on the Fortune 500 list, in addition to many other large to mid-size companies. It’s biggest benefit is that it can fuel an entire enterprise’s needs, from payroll to ecommerce and numerous other business needs that involve tech. So, that’s why it’s still around. 

This is an exciting time for me, and for the business, and I love that I get paid to work there while learning a TON about tech and how the web works.

snippet.title: ⭕The one book I regret not having as a beginning web developer || Jon Duckett JavaScript & jQuery
snippet.description:
As self-taught web developers, we understand the need for quality educational investments. With the high costs of bootcamps, colleges, and online courses that still leave a lot of developers unemployed, even the most educated of developers often find themselves exploring the internet for additional resources. 

My gateway into web development were two books by Mark Myers. He is the author of the Smarter Way Series, and both his HTML/CSS book along with his JavaScript book advanced my learning like no other materials before it. They were also a really good deal at less than twenty dollars each. 

Then there was the Jon Duckett JavaScript & jQuery book. I'd heard a LOT of great things about it...But $40? Come on, now. That was a little expensive for me, especially since I was't 100% sure I wanted to do this as a career. 

Fast forward two years, and I finally got around to snagging it. My only regret? That I didn't buy it when I was an aspiring web developer. This is a beautiful book that is absolutely packed with must-know web development concepts concerning JavaScript and jQuery. And even though it's 2018 and we're looking away from jQuery, it still has its uses (it's also used a lot in previous coding projects, so knowledge of it is still important). 

In this video, I give a little show and tell of this book, and what I love about it.

snippet.title: ⭕ Do web developers need to know graphic design? || How to compete with low-cost web developers

snippet.title: ⭕I drove 7 hours for a web development interview AND GOT THE JOB || Web Developer Jobs
snippet.description:
I GOT THE JOB! A few weeks ago, I got a callback for a web developer job interview. It was a job I was really interested in — the company was small, the company was growing, and it sounded like they were going to be working on some pretty cool projects. ***open me*** 
The catch: NONE of their tech stack matched with mine. 

Every bit of it was just one tiny degree away from what I develop with. 

They use Vue. 

I use React. 

They use DB2. 

I use MySQL. 

They use OO PHP. 

I use OO JavaScript.

 Despite that, I got the callback!  

The second catch? I lived seven hours away, and they wanted to do an interview. The senior developer at the company told me we could do a phone interview if it was too much trouble. But I needed to make an impression. I needed to put myself ahead of the pack! 

Because, remember, I have never worked with any of their tech stack. So, I drove seven hours to meet with them. That night, I checked into my hotel in this new city, studied a bit, and woke up the next day, nervous as heck but there was no way I could bail out. I had already invested a few hundred bucks in the rental car, hotel, food, and fun little trinkets (trinkets = buying local high school sports team tee shirts at Saver’s.). 

At the company entrance, I was greeted by the owner of the company, and we went into another room to start the interview. The senior web developer and a third guy (a DBA [database administrator] or network guy, I can’t really recall) joined us. 

The rest is history, or at least in an upcoming blog post. :) 

In this video, I show you why I traveled all that way to interview with a tech company, and how it put me ahead of all the other candidates. 

I GOT THE JOB!

snippet.title: How to do a UX review || Real-life website critique
snippet.description:
Having somebody review your work is absolutely anxiety-inducing. Just thinking about the prospect of somebody dissecting my creation is enough to give me vomitific sensations! **open me**

While reviews can be intimidating, they're also one of the best tools available to quickly improve your product or creative work. It can be a portfolio, video, code, a website -- doesn't matter. In a professional review setting, the reviewer is tearing apart your work for one goal, and one goal only: for you to improve. If you can withstand the criticism, you will be well on your way to improving your creations. And that means more people who will pay attention to you. More clicks, engagements, likes. More money. Just....More!

Today I'm reviewing a subscriber's website, who has bravely and kindly agreed to let me share the critique with the world to help others also improve. His website is filled with impressive projects, but as you'll see in the video, there are a few issues that need to be addressed for maximum UX/UI. We'll go over those, using the gold standard in UX/UI assessment, "10 Heuristics for User Interface Design" by Jakob Nielsen. It's very important to use a standard when reviewing, otherwise it just turns into a subjective review (consisting of basic comments like "Dude, I love this picture!")...And that helps nobody.

Thank you Eric for asking me to review your site! I can't wait to see what improvements you make to it and I am looking forward to checking it out soon! RTC

snippet.title: ⭕MEET THE 3COM ERGO AUDREY
snippet.description:
I recently came across this strange little device that was manufactured in the year 2000. Is this a prototype that's ahead of its time, or just another example of e-waste? ***open me***
The 3com Audrey was a standalone web browser, coldly referred to as an Internet appliance. Simply plug 'er in, plug it in to your Internet box, and wait for the unit to automatically dial your ISP. Well, I didn't have any way to connect the Audrey to make that all-important communication, so instead I was forced to have some offline fun with the large TV-like 'channel' changer which selected preset websites for you (don't worry, you can also make your own channels). The Audrey also has a well-appointed email button next to the channel changer. 

BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE. A clear acrylic stylus to make you feel all-so-hip? Check. A wireless keyboard? Check. (They had wireless in 2000? Dope.). Perhaps the biggest selling point, the unit even includes a hearty Blue Screen of Death upon checking email (sarc). 

What's so interesting about items like these is that although they look like absolute e-waste these days, it resembles an early iPad prototype. And I think that's an important lesson in tech, because nothing is ever made totally from scratch -- tech is incremental, iterative, and takes ideas from earlier attempts at maybe not-so-ready-for-primetime products. The Audrey is kind of useless these days, but what if it just had a few more accoutrements, like WiFi capabilities, or a nice battery to keep it ticking while its users are on the move? We might be calling the iPad the Audreypad.

snippet.title: Technical Phone Interview: What I experienced as a web developer
snippet.description:
You think the first interview is anxiety-inducing? Just you wait 'til you get to the technical phone interview. There aren't any markers, whiteboards, or body language from your interviewer telling you if you're on the right track: it's just you getting thrown a series of questions to test if you're the right fit for the job. 

I *just* got out of a technical phone interview for a fullstack web position, and share my experiences in this video. There were between 15-20 interview questions ranging from basic CSS and JavaScript stuff, to questions about relational databases including the difference between inner and outer joins (I froze up!). 

This video also explains how I spent a lot of time researching questions for job interviews that are more geared to mid-level and senior-level development positions, when I should have been focused more on the web development basics (since I'm currently a junior dev and looking for that kind of position). 

Normally your interviewer will start with some softball questions to warm you up, and it's important to get those right since it's going to build trust in the interviewer to proceed. In other words, let him know you know your stuff in the first couple questions, and it just might be OK to stumble once the questions start getting harder, or just catch you off guard. Heck, not all of us actively develop in jQuery, and even the easy stuff can be easy to forget when you're asked to talk about it. 

Enjoy the video!

snippet.title: ⭕Artificial Intelligence will steal her job
snippet.description:
Artificial Intelligence will STEAL her job...And I couldn't be happier.

There's been a lot of talk lately about how artificial intelligence will be taking your job. Like, YOUR job. Is it hype, or is there truth to it? The current technology stack used by web developers, AI devs, and other tech types support the idea that automation 2.0 could be coming to a job near you very soon. Time to PANIC, right? Well, maybe not. 

Lots of people actually don't like their job, and would rather be doing something else. *That* is one of the biggest reasons to open one's mind to the idea of artificial intelligence. The idea is that people will finally be able to do what they actually enjoy while the robots do all the dirty work for us. And hey, that ain't such a bad deal -- go fishing, spending time with mom, and enjoy life without the stress of having to deal with bosses, paperwork, and broken water coolers. You might be wondering, "Yeah, great, but how can I afford to enjoy my life?" Well, the idea behind AI on a massive, job-stealing scale is that you receive a payment as part of a system called Universal Basic Income (UBI), to supplement your income you may make from your other pursuits...You know, the  ones you enjoy. While still a fantasy, the idea behind UBI is that people are paid a cut of the money that robots earn, while the robots continue to press on with their tasks. Because, after all, robots don't need to eat, go to medical appointments, or otherwise need a paycheck for basic living. But people? Yeah, we need money for that stuff. 

And that's where the big problem also comes from: Will governments be equitable in ensuring the UBI is given to their citizens? 
Very good question. We don't know.
